newsitem.title: UK: Dual protease combination hits HIV hard - study.
newsitem.headline: Dual protease combination hits HIV hard - study.

text.p: A combination of two AIDS drugs known as protease inhibitors works better than any drug treatment yet to knock out the HIV virus, researchers reported on Wednesday.
Putting together Abbott Laboratories' ritonavir (Norvir) and Hoffmann-La Roche's saquinavir (Invirase) reduced the virus by 99.9 percent, the two companies announced.
"This represents the most potent and complete suppression of HIV infection achieved by any regimen to date," said Bill Cameron of the University of Ottawa, who worked on the study.
"The great majority of patients have cleared the virus from their bloodstream in three months time."

Most researchers attending the Third International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection, being held in Birmingham, agree that using three or even four drugs against the HIV virus is the most effective way to suppress it.
But Cameron said his group's findings showed there were other alternatives.
"What we do see is as near-complete an anti-viral response in patients as has been achieved in any other study," he told Reuters.

AIDS drugs target the virus at various stages of its cycle of replication. Protease inhibitors attack the virus late in the cycle, causing it to produce immature copies of itself which cannot infect other cells.

Cameron warned that his group's study was only 20 weeks old, so there was no way to tell if the two-drug combination would work over the long-term. He said it was also not certain that simply knocking levels of the virus back was enough to make the patient better.
The 140 patients from several cities were given various doses of the two drugs. None had been given protease inhibitors before and all were only moderately infected.

In a second announcement on Wednesday, Roche said it would start working with rival Agouron Pharmaceuticals Inc of La Jolla, California, to test a combination of saquinavir with Agouron's nelfinavir (Viracept), another protease inhibitor.
Volunteers will be recruited for the study in Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland, France, Germany and Britain.

Raffi Babakhanian of the AIDS Treatment Project in London, who campaigns for greater availability of AIDS drugs, said the test was important for patients who could not tolerate other classes of drugs or who had become resistant to them.
"Finally, there are patients for whom triple therapy is not enough to reduce viral load below detectable levels," he said.
